qs.q: A 28-year-old man suffers a displaced talar neck fracture following a high-velocity fall. He is counseled regarding a high risk of avascular necrosis of the talar body. Which vascular feature of the talus accounts for this risk?
o: Antegrade blood supply entering proximally at the posterior process
Retrograde blood supply entering distally and flowing proximally
Complete absence of capsular and ligamentous extraosseous flow
Total reliance on intra-articular synovial diffusion for nutrition
qs.e: The talus receives its predominant blood supply in a retrograde manner, with vessels entering distally at the tarsal canal and neck to supply the proximal body. Disruption of these distal vessels during a talar neck fracture deprives the proximal body of perfusion, whereas an antegrade flow would have spared it.

qs.q: A patient sustains a fracture of the neck of the femur and is informed of an increased risk of avascular necrosis. Which vessel group is primarily responsible for supplying the femoral head?
o: Descending genicular branches arising from femoral artery
Retinacular vessels arising from the extracapsular ring
Acetabular branches arising directly from obturator artery
Internal pudendal branches arising via lesser sciatic foramen
qs.e: The femoral head is supplied by retinacular vessels arising from an extracapsular arterial ring formed by the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries. Damage to these vessels during a femoral neck fracture leads to avascular necrosis.

es.q: Discuss the morphology and clinical outcomes of osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis).
es.m:
- **Common causes:** Includes fractures, corticosteroid use, alcohol abuse, sickle cell crisis, bisphosphonate therapy, radiation, Gaucher disease, and dysbarism.
- **Medullary infarcts:** Characterized as geographic regions with trabecular bone and marrow necrosis, where collateral blood flow limits cortical involvement.
- **Subchondral infarcts:** Present as wedge or triangular shapes where the overlying cartilage survives because it is nourished by synovial fluid.
- **Histology of dead bone:** Shows empty lacunae alongside necrotic adipocytes, with calcium soaps forming from released fatty acids.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Avascular necrosis (AVN) is death of bone tissue due to loss of blood supply, most often affecting the femoral head. Early recognition and staging guide treatment to preserve joint function.

sections.p: AVN is bone death caused by interruption of arterial flow, leading to marrow fat cell death and collapse of subchondral bone.
b: Diagnosis requires imaging (MRI > X‑ray) plus clinical history of risk factors.

t.b: Does the bone show a double‑line sign? Positive indicates early AVN before radiographic changes.
Is there subchondral lucency or crescent sign? Positive suggests later stage disease.

sections.p: The most used system is the Ficat‑Arlet classification, ranging from stage I (MRI only) to stage IV (joint collapse with arthritis).
b: Stage I: normal X‑ray, MRI abnormal.
Stage II: sclerosis or cysts on X‑ray, no collapse.
Stage III: subchondral fracture (crescent sign), early collapse.
Stage IV: secondary osteoarthritis.

sections.p: AVN results from any condition that blocks blood flow to bone.
b: Trauma (femoral neck fracture) – most common acute cause.
Chronic steroid use – frequent in low‑resource settings for asthma, nephrotic syndrome.
Alcohol excess – especially binge drinking.
Sickle cell disease – vaso‑occlusion in marrow.
HIV infection or antiretroviral therapy.
Tuberculosis of the hip or femur.
Malaria‑related sequestration in endemic areas.

sections.p: Patients report deep, progressive joint pain that worsens with weight‑bearing and improves with rest, often with limited range of motion.
b: Pain initially intermittent, later constant.
Crepitus or grinding may appear as collapse occurs.

sections.p: Imaging is central; labs help identify underlying causes.
b: Blood count, ESR/CRP to rule out infection.
Lipid profile if steroid‑induced AVN suspected.

t.b: Is there anemia or leukocytosis? Helps detect sickle cell crisis or infection.
Elevated triglycerides support steroid‑related AVN pathophysiology.

sections.p: Unchecked AVN can lead to joint collapse, secondary osteoarthritis, and loss of ambulation.
b: Sudden increase in pain indicating fracture.
Rapid loss of hip motion suggesting collapse.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, protect the joint, and consider surgical options when collapse is advanced.
b: Stop steroids if possible; switch to steroid‑sparing agents.
Limit weight‑bearing and use crutches.
Bisphosphonates (e.g., alendronate) to reduce bone resorption – avoid in renal failure.
Core decompression for early stages.
Total hip arthroplasty for stage III‑IV disease.

sections.p: Regular clinical review and imaging every 6‑12 months monitor progression.
b: Encourage smoking cessation and moderate alcohol.
Manage sickle cell with hydroxyurea to reduce vaso‑occlusion.
Screen high‑risk patients (steroid users, trauma) early with MRI.

sections.p: Conditions that cause hip pain and limited motion may mimic AVN.
b: Transient osteoporosis of the hip – pain resolves, no collapse.
Septic arthritis – inflammatory signs, positive joint fluid culture.
Hip osteoarthritis – joint space narrowing without necrosis.

sections.p: Early disease may have normal X‑ray, leading to false reassurance.
b: Normal plain film does not exclude AVN; MRI is required if suspicion remains.
Elevated ESR/CRP may be absent in non‑infectious AVN, so normal values do not rule out disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening hip pain with inability to bear weight
New onset fever with joint pain

faq.q: Why is MRI preferred over X‑ray in early AVN?
faq.a: MRI detects marrow edema and the double‑line sign before any bone changes appear on X‑ray.
In early stages, core decompression and off‑loading may halt progression, but many patients eventually need joint replacement.

faq.q: Is alcohol a direct cause of AVN?
faq.a: Chronic heavy drinking raises fat emboli risk and impairs blood flow, making it a recognized risk factor.
